newsitem.title: USA: Japan, Germany cited for exporting measles to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Germany cited for exporting measles to U.S.

text.p: Lax vaccination practices for measles in Japan and Germany have set back the U.S. goal of eliminating the contagious disease, researchers said on Tuesday.

A total of 43 U.S. cases of measles between 1992 and 1994 were traced back to Japan and Germany. Only one U.S. case since 1994 was found to have originated in Latin America as a result of an effort by health authorities to eradicate the virus in the Americas by 2000.
Prior to 1990, Mexico had been a prime source of measles imported into the United States, researchers at the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta said.

"The emergence of Japan and Germany as major sources of imported measles to the United States suggests ongoing measles transmission in these highly industrialised countries, which have less intensive measles control efforts than countries in the Western Hemisphere," Charles Vitek of the CDC wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

The report said Japan did not require measles vaccination for school entry and only two-thirds of 1-year-olds in Japan had received a single dose of the vaccine in 1993. In Germany, just three-quarters of the population had received one dose of the vaccine, although two doses are generally recommended.

The CDC previously reported 488 U.S. measles cases in 1996 and 301 in 1995, the lowest number since measles became a notifiable disease in 1912. About two-thirds of the 1996 cases were related to international travel.

The incidents were down sharply from 1990, when 27,786 cases were reported during a resurgence of the disease. But researchers said as long as measles can be imported strains of the virus can re-establish themselves in the Americas.

They suggested U.S. citizens not immune to measles should be required to get vaccinated before travelling overseas, and foreign citizens entering the United States should either have a record of vaccination or be inoculated before entering.
